paragraphs.heading: What plants are
paragraphs.text: Plants are the eukaryotic organisms that make up the kingdom Plantae. Most get their energy from sunlight, using the green pigment chlorophyll in their chloroplasts to make sugars from carbon dioxide and water. Over time some plants have instead become parasites, taking energy from other organisms. Most plants are made of many cells; the exceptions are glaucophytes, some green algae and a few red algae.

paragraphs.heading: A shrinking kingdom
paragraphs.text: In Aristotle's biology every living thing was either a plant or an animal, so the plant kingdom held everything that was not an animal, including algae and fungi. Aristotle set beings with a sensitive soul apart from plants, which had only a vegetative soul. Carl Linnaeus, who laid the basis of modern scientific classification, still kept the two kingdoms. Definitions have narrowed since, and today fungi and some algae are left out. One definition treats plants as the green plants, the green algae plus the land plants, which run from mosses and ferns to conifers and flowering plants.

paragraphs.heading: How many, how big
paragraphs.text: There are about 382,000 accepted plant species, and around 283,000 of them produce seeds. Flowering plants make up about 85 to 90 percent of all plant species. In size, plants range from single cells such as picozoa, less than 3 micrometres across, to giant trees like the conifer Sequoia sempervirens, which can grow 120 metres tall.

paragraphs.heading: Why plants matter
paragraphs.text: Green plants supply a large share of the world's oxygen. The sugars they make by photosynthesis power most of Earth's ecosystems, and animals and other organisms either eat plants or depend on them in other ways. Grain, fruit and vegetables are basic human foods that people have domesticated over thousands of years. People also use plants for building materials such as wood, for ornaments, for writing materials and for a great variety of medicines. The scientific study of plants is called botany.

paragraphs.heading: From water to land
paragraphs.text: Land plants come from ancestors that lived in water. A scum of algae formed on land 1,200 million years ago, but the first land plants did not appear until the Ordovician, around 450 million years ago. Early land plants began to diversify in the late Silurian, about 420 million years ago. By the end of the Devonian, most basic features of today's plants were present, including roots, leaves and secondary wood.

paragraphs.heading: Forests, seeds and flowers
paragraphs.text: In the Carboniferous, forests grew in swamps, dominated by clubmosses and horsetails, some of them as big as trees. The first seed plants, early gymnosperms, appeared at this time. Later the Permo-Triassic extinction reshaped living communities, which may have opened the way for flowering plants to evolve in the Triassic, around 200 million years ago. Their spread in the Cretaceous was so fast that Charles Darwin called it an abominable mystery.

paragraphs.heading: Inside a plant cell
paragraphs.text: Plant cells have features that animal cells lack: a large central vacuole filled with water, chloroplasts, and a strong but flexible cell wall outside the cell membrane. Chloroplasts come from a partnership that once existed between a cell that could not photosynthesize and photosynthetic cyanobacteria. The cell wall, made mostly of cellulose, lets a plant cell swell up with water without bursting.
